title: This Bird's Wings Are Made for Sharp Turns
summary:
The European nightjar is a bird that hunts insects at night. Every year, it flies thousands of miles between Europe and southern Africa.

You might think a bird that travels so far would have wings made for flying fast. But scientists at Lund University found something different.

They studied nightjars in a wind tunnel. The birds have broad wing tips. These help them make sharp turns while flying slowly to catch insects. But when the birds fly fast, their wings make lift less well. Lift is the force that helps keep a bird in the air.

Scientist Christoffer Johansson said the wings are "a compromise," a mix that balances different needs.

The team found a surprise, too. When the nightjar raises its wings, it still pushes itself forward. Scientists had mainly seen this in bats and insects.

This idea could help engineers build better flying robots and drones. Next, the team wants to know if other birds do the same thing.
why_it_matters: Learning how birds fly could help engineers build better drones you might see one day.
